# Page 1^page=1
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Software Engineering 2 Alloy Part 1: Introduction First example: the address book Second example: the family tree

# Page 2^page=2
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy part 1 Introduction 2

# Page 3^page=3
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy Resources • The book is the main resource • New, work-in-progress book freely available at: https://practicalalloy.github.io/index.html • Other material: https://alloytools.org • Tool • Documentation • Examples • Tutorial • “Some slides are adapted from Greg Dennis and Rob Seater Software Design Group, MIT” 3

# Page 4^page=4
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy • Alloy is a formal notation for specifying models of systems and software • Looks like a declarative OO language • But also has a strong mathematical foundation • Alloy comes with a supporting tool to • Simulate specifications and • Perform formal verification of properties = (bounded) model checking • Note • We refer to version 6 (last version) of the Alloy language and tool • Some small, but important, modifications w.r.t. version 5 • Some additional concepts, which will be illustrated at the end of this part 4

# Page 5^page=5
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy — Declarative Modeling • Alloy is used for abstractions and conceptual modeling in a declarative manner • Declarative approach to programming and modeling: • “declarative programming is a programming paradigm that expresses the logic of a computation without describing its control flow” • “describing what the program should accomplish, rather than describing how to go about accomplishing it” 5

# Page 6^page=6
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy — Applications for SE • In RE Alloy can be used to formally describe • the domain and its properties, or • operations that the machine must provide • In software design to formally model components and their interactions 6

# Page 7^page=7
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy — Automated Analysis • Any real-life system has a set of properties and constraints • Automated formal verification of specifications can help check whether or not the properties will be satisfied by the system and the constraints will never be violated 7 “The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.” ~ Richard P. Feynman

# Page 8^page=8
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Formal verification — successful stories • Intel has been using model checking to verify correctness of operations implemented by CPUs 8 • NASA has been using model checking techniques to verify executable source code used in their space missions

# Page 9^page=9
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi What is Alloy? • First order predicate logic + relational calculus • Carefully chosen subset of relational algebra • uniform model for individuals, sets and relations • no higher-order relations • Almost no arithmetic • Modules and hierarchies • New in Alloy 6: mutable sets and relations • Suitable for small, exploratory specifications • Powerful and fast analysis tool • is this specification satisfiable? is this predicate true? 9

# Page 10^page=10
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy part 1 The AddressBook example: Atoms Relations Predicates and Assertions 10

# Page 11^page=11
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Let’s Get Started! • Suppose we are asked to model very simple address books • Books contain a bunch of addresses linked to the corresponding names Names Addresses Books What to model? How to model? 11

# Page 12^page=12
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi AddressBook in Alloy • Name and Addr are two types of entities • Book is another type of entity • addr links Name to Addr within the context of Book • It is a ternary relation b -> n -> a • keyword lone: each Name can correspond to at most one Addr sig Name, Addr {} sig Book { addr: Name -> lone Addr } set any number one exactly one lone zero or one some one or more 12

# Page 13^page=13
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Logic: relations of atoms • Atoms are Alloy's primitive entities • indivisible, immutable, uninterpreted • Relations associate atoms with one another • set of tuples, tuples are sequences of atoms 13

# Page 14^page=14
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Relations • Relation = set of ordered n-tuples of atoms • n is called the arity of the relation • Relations in Alloy are typed • Determined by the declaration of the relation • Example: a relation with type Person -> String only contains pairs • whose first component is a Person • and whose second component is a String 14

# Page 15^page=15
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Logic: Everything is a Relation • Sets are unary (1 column) relations • Scalars are singleton sets • Ternary relation Name = {(N0), Addr = {(A0), Book = {(B0), (N1), (A1), (B1)} (N2)} (A2)} myName = {(N1)} yourName = {(N2)} myBook = {(B0)} addr = {(B0, N0, A0), (B0, N1, A1), (B1, N1, A2), (B1, N2, A2)} what is myName.(Book.addr)? 15

# Page 16^page=16
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi myName.(Book.addr) addr = { (B0, N0, A0), (B0, N1, A1), (B1, N1, A2), (B1, N2, A2)} Book = { (B0), (B1)} Book.addr = { (N0, A0), (N1, A1), (N1, A2), (N2, A2)} Book.addr = { (N0, A0), (N1, A1), (N1, A2), (N2, A2)} myName = { (N1)} myName.(Book.addr) = { (A1), (A2),} 16

# Page 17^page=17
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Static Analysis • Let’s open the Alloy tool and play a bit! • We add an empty predicate show by using keyword pred to find the instances of the entities involved in the modeling • In this case, the state exploration is limited to 3 for each entity except Book that is set to 1 pred show {} run show for 3 but 1 Book 17

# Page 18^page=18
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Static Analysis (cont.) • Adding a constraint on the number of (Name,Address) relations in a given book • Constraining the number of different addresses that appear in the book • Can we fulfil the constraint below? pred show [b: Book] { #b.addr > 1 } pred show [b: Book] { #b.addr > 1 #Name.(b.addr) > 1 } pred show [b: Book] { #b.addr > 1 some n: Name | #n.(b.addr) > 1 } 18

# Page 19^page=19
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Dynamic Analysis (old style, but compatible with Alloy 6) • Let’s model some operations... • A predicate that adds an address and name to a book • b and bpost model two versions of the book, respectively before and after the operation • Operations can be invoked pred add [b, bpost: Book, n: Name, a: Addr] { bpost.addr = b.addr + n -> a } pred showAdd [b, bpost: Book, n: Name, a: Addr] { add[b, bpost, n, a] #Name.(bpost.addr) > 1 } run showAdd 19 Cartesian product (a pair in this case)

# Page 20^page=20
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Dynamic Analysis (cont.) • Deleting a name from the address book pred del [b, bpost: Book, n: Name] { bpost.addr = b.addr - n->Addr } 20

# Page 21^page=21
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Assertions and counterexamples • What happens if we run a delete after an add predicate? Will this take us to the initial state? • Counterexample is a scenario in which the assertion is violated • While checking an assertion, Alloy searches for counterexamples • Do we find a counterexample in this case? assert delUndoesAdd { all b, bpost, bppost: Book, n: Name, a: Addr | add[b, bpost, n, a] and del[bpost, bppost, n] implies b.addr = bppost.addr } check delUndoesAdd for 3 21

# Page 22^page=22
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Resolving the Counterexample • … Yes! When add tries to add a name that already exists and delete will delete the name and the corresponding address • Here is how we can solve the problem: assert delUndoesAdd { all b, bpost, bppost: Book, n: Name, a: Addr | no n.(b.addr) and add[b, bpost, n, a] and del[bpost, bppost, n] implies b.addr = bppost.addr } 22

# Page 23^page=23
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Counterexamples in Alloy • The analysis by Alloy is always bounded to a defined scope • Alloy performs bounded verification • This means that there is NO guarantee that the assertions always hold if no counterexample is found in a certain scope! 23

# Page 24^page=24
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Testing vs Bounded Verification testing: a few cases of arbitrary size bounded verification: all cases within a certain bound 24

# Page 25^page=25
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Functions: An Example • Can we get the addresses in the book corresponding to a certain name? • Example of usage of lookup fun lookup [b: Book, n: Name] : set Addr { n.(b.addr) } assert addLocal { all b, bpost: Book, n1, n2: Name, a: Addr | add[b, bpost, n1, a] and n1 != n2 implies lookup[b, n2] = lookup[bpost, n2] } check addLocal for 3 but 2 Book 25

# Page 26^page=26
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Summary of Alloy Characteristics (1) • An Alloy document is a “source code” unit • It may contain: • Signatures: define types and relationships • Facts: properties of models (constraints!) • Predicates/functions: reusable expressions • Assertions: properties we want to check • Commands: instruct the Alloy Analyzer which assertions to check, and how • A predicate is run to find a world that satisfies it • An assertion is checked to find a counterexample 26

# Page 27^page=27
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Summary of Alloy Characteristics (2) • Signatures, predicates, facts and functions tell how correct worlds (models) are made • When the Alloy analyzer tries to build a model, it must comply with them • Assertions and commands tell which kind of checks must be performed over these worlds • E.g., “find, among all the models, one that violates this assertion” • Of course, the Analyzer cannot check all the (usually infinite) models of a specification • You must also tell the Analyzer how to limit the search 27

# Page 28^page=28
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Alloy part 1 The family tree example: Hierarchies Facts vs predicates Other operators (transitive closure, transpose) 28

# Page 29^page=29
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Family Relationships • There are notions like Person • There are relationships like father, mother, wife, … 29

# Page 30^page=30
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Initial Alloy Model abstract sig Person { father: lone Man, mother: lone Woman } sig Man extends Person { wife: lone Woman } sig Woman extends Person { husband: lone Man } 30 Meta-model

# Page 31^page=31
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Signatures and Fields • Signatures (declared through keyword sig) represent sets of atoms • The fields of a signature are relations whose domain is a subset of the signature • The extends keyword is used to declare a subset of a signature • An abstract signature has no elements except those belonging to the signatures that extend it • m sig A {} : m (e.g., one, some, etc.) declares the multiplicity, the number of elements of A 31

# Page 32^page=32
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Relations • Relations are declared as fields of signatures: • sig A {f : e} • A is the domain • e is the range • You can specify the multiplicity when defining a relation • sig A {f : m e} • The default multiplicity is one 32

# Page 33^page=33
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Can you be your own Grandpa? • Biologically not, but terminologically… let’s check this out: • I’m my own Grandpa! http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eYlJH81dSiw (with family tree) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gkiOm-vmpcY&list=RDgkiOm-vmpcY (with muppets) 33

# Page 34^page=34
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Adding Predicates and Functions • The function grandpas returns the grandfathers of a given person p 34 fun grandpas [p: Person] : set Person { p.(mother+father).father } pred ownGrandpa [p: Person] { p in p.grandpas } This can be written also as p in grandpas[p]

# Page 35^page=35
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Running the Model • The model is executed by trying to see if a predicate is valid for a set of instances of the meta-model 35 run ownGrandpa for 4 Person

# Page 36^page=36
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Fixing some problems in the spec (1) • Issue: Man0 is father of himself • More in general “No one can be his/her own ancestor” 36 Valid model according to the current spec.

# Page 37^page=37
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Fixing some problems in the spec (1) • “No one can be his/her own ancestor” … we need a transitive closure operator 37 fact { no p: Person | p in p.(mother+father) or p in (p.(mother+father)).(mother+father) or p in ((p.(mother+father)).(mother+father)). (mother+father) … }

# Page 38^page=38
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Transitive closure 38 ^ transitive closure * reflexive transitive closure apply only to binary relations Node = {(N0), (N1), (N2), (N3)} next = {(N0, N1), (N1, N2), (N2, N3)} ^next = {(N0, N1), (N0, N2), (N0, N3), (N1, N2), (N1, N3), (N2, N3)} *next = {(N0, N0), (N0, N1), (N0, N2), (N0, N3), (N1, N1), (N1, N2), (N1, N3), (N2, N2), (N2, N3), (N3, N3)} ^r = r + r.r + r.r.r + … *r = iden + ^r first = {(N0)} rest = {(N1), (N2), (N3)} first.^next = rest first.*next = Node sig Node{ next : lone Node } a list the identity relation union

# Page 39^page=39
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Fixing some problems in the spec (2) • “No one can be his/her own ancestor” 39 fact { no p: Person | p in p.^(mother+father) }

# Page 40^page=40
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Fixing some problems in the spec (3) • “If X is husband of Y, then Y is wife of X” • We can express an equivalent constraint through the transpose operator (~) 40 fact { all m: Man, w: Woman | m.wife = w iff w.husband = m }

# Page 41^page=41
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi • Consider the following example • The transpose operator applies only to binary relations • “If X is husband of Y, then Y is wife of X” Transpose operator (~) 41 Node = {(N0), (N1), (N2), (N3)} next = {(N0, N1), (N1, N2), (N2, N3)} ~next = {(N1, N0), (N2, N1), (N3, N2)} fact { wife = ~husband }

# Page 42^page=42
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi More on facts • A fact can contain multiple constraints • The two constraints in the fact are to be considered in and 42 fact { no p: Person | p in p.^(mother+father) wife = ~husband }

# Page 43^page=43
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Are facts different from predicates? • They are both used to express constraints • Facts must hold globally for any atom and relation in the model • Predicates have to be invoked 43

# Page 44^page=44
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Adding Assertions • Check if there is no man who is also his father • Assertions are used to find counterexamples which are the instances of a model 44 assert NoSelfFather { no m: Man | m = m.father } check NoSelfFather

# Page 45^page=45
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Adding more facts to the model • Social convention: it is not possible that someone has a wife or husband who is also one of his/her ancestors 45 fact SocialConvention { no ((wife+husband) & ^(mother+father)) } intersection facts can be named for readability purposes

# Page 46^page=46
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Adding more facts to the model • Other issues: Still, wife and husband can have common ancestors! 46

# Page 47^page=47
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi How to avoid that wives and husbands have common ancestors? • Does this solve the common ancestor problem? • To which fact is this equivalent? • Answer: SocialConvention 47 fact SocialConvention2 { all m: Man, w: Woman | ( m.wife = w and w.husband = m ) implies not( m in w.^(father+mother) or w in m.^(father+mother) ) }

# Page 48^page=48
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Another solution 48 fun ancestors [p: Person]: set Person { p.^(mother+father) } fact noCommonAncestors { all p1: Man, p2: Woman | p1->p2 in wife implies ancestors[p1] & ancestors[p2] = none } • Check yourself if it works Cartesian product (a pair in this case) empty set

# Page 49^page=49
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Other solution (?) 49 fact SocialConvention3 { no ( (wife+husband) & (mother+father).~(mother+father) ) } • noCommonAncestors is stronger than SocialConvention3

# Page 50^page=50
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Proof" that noCommonAncestor is stronger than SocialConvention3 50 pred noCommonAncestors { all p1: Man, p2: Woman | p1->p2 in wife implies ancestors[p1] & ancestors[p2] = none } pred SocialConvention3 { no ((wife+husband) & (mother+father).~(mother+father)) } Notice the declaration

# Page 51^page=51
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Proof" (cont.) 51 assert Stronger { noCommonAncestors implies SocialConvention3 } check Stronger for 8 assert NotStronger { SocialConvention3 implies noCommonAncestors } check NotStronger for 8

# Page 52^page=52
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Still, we can have this case 52 Man1 is father and, at the same time, grandpa of Man0.

# Page 53^page=53
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Does this address the problem? 53 fact SocialConvention4 { all p1: Person, p2: Person | p1 in p2.(mother+father) implies p1.(mother+father) & p2.(mother+father) = none }

# Page 54^page=54
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Software Engineering 2 Alloy Part 2: New features: mutable relations and sets

# Page 55^page=55
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi From unmutable relations… • Let's go back to the address book example: • Describing the evolution of the address book following additions and deletions required to explicitly represent the address book before and after the operation, because it was unmutable: 55 sig Name, Addr {} sig Book { addr: Name -> lone Addr } pred add [b, bpost: Book, n: Name, a: Addr] { bpost.addr = b.addr + n -> a }

# Page 56^page=56
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi … to mutable ones • What if we can say that relation addr changes over time? • Now, we can have that an address book initially (first instant) is empty, then, after that (i.e., in the second instant) it has 1 address, then, after that (i.e., in the third instant) it has 2 addresses 56 sig Name, Addr {} sig Book { var addr: Name -> lone Addr } new keyword, it means the relation is mutable

# Page 57^page=57
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi • We show an address book whose size increases in the first 3 instants: pred show [b: Book] { #b.addr = 0 after ( #b.addr = 1 and after #b.addr = 2 ) } Evolution of an address book 57 It means "at the next instant" pred show [b: Book] { #b.addr = 0 ; #b.addr = 1 ; #b.addr = 2 } • It can be also written, more succintly, with the "sequence" operator (;)

# Page 58^page=58
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Let us run the predicate 58 We say how many instants we want to represent run show for 3 but 1 Book, 3 steps These are the first 2 instants (the white ones)

# Page 59^page=59
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi New add and delete 59 pred add [b: Book, n: Name, a: Addr] { b.addr' = b.addr + n -> a } pred del [b: Book, n: Name] { b.addr' = b.addr - n->Addr } It means "the next value of b.addr"

# Page 60^page=60
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi New assertion • This assertion means "if in the first instant n does not belong to b, and n is added to b, and then, at the next instant (i.e., the second) n is removed from b, then address book b after 2 instants is the same as the initial one" 60 assert delUndoesAdd { all b: Book, n: Name, a: Addr | no n.(b.addr) and add[b, n, a] and after del[b, n] implies b.addr = b.addr'' } check delUndoesAdd for 5 steps This means "b.addr after 2 instants"

# Page 61^page=61
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi assert alwDelUndoesAdd { all b: Book, n: Name, a: Addr | always ( no n.(b.addr) and (add[b, n, a] ; del[b, n]) implies b.addr = b.addr'' ) } "Always" • What if we want to say that "at all time instants, if n does not belong to b and n is added…"? • We can say "always, if …": 62 new operator First instant Second instant Third instant … always F = true in i iff F = true for each time instant k >= i

# Page 62^page=62
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example to illustrate temporal operators (h/t L. Padalino, F. P. Panaccione, F. Santambrogio: github.com/lucapada/ResearchProjectAlloy6) • Consider the following signature 63 sig Device { var status: DevStatus } enum DevStatus { Working, Broken } Useful abbreviation to avoid declaring the abstract signatures

# Page 63^page=63
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Some temporal constraints • Once broken, a device can never be repaired 64 Working Working Broken …Examples Broken Broken Working Working …Working Working fact NoRepair { all d: Device | always ( d.status = Broken implies after always d.status = Broken ) }

# Page 64^page=64
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi eventually operator • If a device is working, it will eventually break 65 fact NotAlwaysFunctioning { all d: Device | always ( d.status = Working implies eventually d.status = Broken ) } Example Working Working …Working Working Broken eventually F = true in i iff F = true for some time instant k>=i

# Page 65^page=65
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Past" operators: historically • If a device is working, it has been working since the beginning 66 fact NowWorkingPreviouslyWorking { all d: Device | always ( d.status = Working implies historically d.status = Working ) } Example Working… Working Working historically F = true in i iff F = true for each time instant k<=i

# Page 66^page=66
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Past" operators: before • This is equivalent to NowWorkingPreviouslyWorking 67 fact NowWorkingPreviouslyWorking2 { all d: Device | after always ( d.status = Working implies before d.status = Working ) } It means "the previous instant"

# Page 67^page=67
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Evaluating before in the first instant • The first instant does not have a previous instant, so by definition before F in the first instant is false, no matter the formula F 68 First instant Second instant Third instant … Here "before" is the first instant Here "before" is the second instant Here we do not have a "before" instant We evaluate the formula starting from one instant after the first one (i.e., from the second instant) fact NowWorkingPreviouslyWorking2 { all d: Device | after always ( d.status = Working implies before d.status = Working ) }

# Page 68^page=68
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Past" operators: once • Let us introduce a predicate • If a device is broken, it must have broken sometime in the past 69 pred break[ d: Device ] { d.status = Working d.status' = Broken } fact IfBrokenDidBreak { all d: Device | always ( d.status = Broken implies once break[d] ) }

# Page 69^page=69
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi "Past" operators: once • If a device is broken, it must have broken sometime in the past 70 fact IfBrokenDidBreak { all d: Device | always ( d.status = Broken implies once break[d] ) } once F = true in i iff F = true for some time instant k<=i Example BrokenWorking break Broken

# Page 70^page=70
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi FUTURE PAST always historically eventually once after before 34 Temporal operators*: summary * For details and other operators, you can watch this video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GncsAmy29l0 71

# Page 71^page=71
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example: message deletion from mailbox • Model a system handling messages, which can be deleted from a mailbox and later restored • We introduce the notion of "trash", from which messages can be restored • Some messages are in the trash (i.e., they are trashed), others are not 72

# Page 72^page=72
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Signatures 73 var sig Message {} var sig Trashed in Message {} Signatures (i.e., sets of elements) can also be mutable Some messages are in the Trashed set. Signatures are mutable, which means that a message can be "regular", then be trashed, then be regular again, etc. This states that Trashed is a subset (not necessarily a proper one) of Message, i.e., Trashed ⊆ Message holds in allows subsets to be overlapping, unlike extends m1 m2 m3 m4 Trashed Message Second instantFirst instant m1 m2 m3 m4Trashed Message m1 m2 m3 m4 Trashed Message Third instant

# Page 73^page=73
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Predicates • Deletion operation • Predicate capturing the condition that a message can be restored • Restore operation 74 pred delete[ m: Message ] { m not in Trashed Trashed' = Trashed + m Message' = Message } The subset with the trashed messages changes, while the total set of messages does not pred restore[ m: Message ] { restoreEnabled[m] Trashed' = Trashed - m Message' = Message } pred restoreEnabled[ m:Message ] { m in Trashed }

# Page 74^page=74
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Predicates (2) • Change in system state: trash is emptied • Predicate representing the fact that the state of the system does not change • Change in system state: new message arrives 75 pred deleteTrashed { #Trashed > 0 after #Trashed = 0 Message' = Message-Trashed } pred receiveMessages { #Message' > #Message Message in Message' Trashed' = Trashed } pred doNothing { Message' = Message Trashed' = Trashed }

# Page 75^page=75
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Behavior of the system 76 fact systemBehavior { no Trashed always ( ( some m: Message | delete[m] or restore[m] ) or deleteTrashed or receiveMessages or doNothing ) } Initially the trash is empty Several things can occur during system execution: • a message could be deleted or restored • the trash could be emptied • new messages could arrive • nothing happens in the system (no state change)

# Page 76^page=76
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Assertions (do you think they hold?) • If a message is restored, sometimes in the past it had to be deleted • If at a certain point in time all messages are trashed and the trash is emptied, then, from that point on there will be no more messages 77 assert restoreAfterDelete { all m: Message | always restore[m] implies once delete[m] } assert deleteAll { always ( ( Message in Trashed and deleteTrashed ) implies after always no Message) }

# Page 77^page=77
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi More assertions (do these hold?) • The set of messages never changes • If no messages are ever deleted, then the trash will never be emptied 78 assert messagesNeverChange { always (Message' in Message and Message in Message') } assert ifMessagesNotDeletedTrashNotEmptied { ( always all m : Message | not delete[m] ) implies always not deleteTrashed }
